notes.claim: Regulation 433.1.1 requires In not less than Ib, In not above the lowest Iz of the circuit conductors, and I2 not above 1.45 Iz; the slides write the first two as Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz.

Anything that makes the cable artificially warm, such as thermal insulation or a higher ambient temperature, needs a rating factor; Ca is for ambient temperature, Cg for grouping and Ci for thermal insulation.

Rating factors are applied as divisors to In, giving the tabulated current It the cable needs; It is the tabulated figure for a single circuit at the table's ambient, while Iz is the capacity as installed.
Only factors that act together are combined; the slides' 3 kW heater gives It = 21.2 A (Ca and Cg) and 19.3 A (Ca and Ci) and designs to the higher, on the reference method with the lowest Iz.
A device's I2 is typically 1.45 times In (a 10 A type B breaker: 14.5 A), and the cable must withstand it: for Iz = 13 A the check is I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz, that is 14.5 against 18.85 A.
A semi-enclosed (rewireable) BS 3036 fuse has an I2 that can be up to 2 × Iz, so its In must not exceed 0.725 × Iz, which the slides put in as Cf = 0.725.

Circuit-breaker types B, C and D relate to the start-up current of the circuit; the assignment asks for cables from the starter to the motor to be chosen on delta running conditions and other factors present.

Table 4B1 in his copy of BS 7671 has no 20 °C row: it starts at 25 °C, where the factor for 90 °C thermosetting cable is 1.02 (1.00 at 30 °C). Below 30 °C the factor is above 1; a 20 °C ambient has no value in the book, so the lesson uses a labelled practice value (1.00, which takes no credit for the cool room).
Appendix 4 of BS 7671 is informative, and other methods (for example a cable maker's own data) are legitimate, so the tables are taught as the usual way to show compliance, not the only one.

Six single-core conductors from a star-delta starter all carry the winding current in delta running; Table 4C1 treats n single-core cables as n/3 circuits of three loaded conductors, so six singles are two three-phase circuits, and bunched and enclosed, two circuits give Cg = 0.80.

A thermal overload relay in the delta circuit of a star-delta starter is set to 0.58 times the motor In (the winding current) and must not be set higher than it, so the starter-to-motor cables are sized on 23.08 A ÷ √3 = 13.33 A, not on the line current (a relay in the incoming line, as in the Schneider type 2 coordination, is set to the full motor In instead).

Table 4E1A (90 °C thermosetting singles, copper), Reference Method B, the column for 3 or 4 loaded cables on three-phase AC, gives 15 A for 1 mm² and 20 A for 1.5 mm²; Reference Method B is conduit on a wall or in trunking, and the IET adds that a conduit fixed to a masonry wall may carry more than the tabulated value.

Circuit-breaker type follows the starting current: type B trips instantaneously at 3 to 5 In, type C at 5 to 10 In (suited to small motors and fluorescent-lighting surges) and type D at 10 to 20 In (high inrush); a motor takes a much higher current starting than running, so a device must be chosen not to trip on it, and the standard breaker ratings include 25 A.

A star-delta start draws roughly 2 to 2.7 times full-load current against 6 to 8 times for direct-on-line (a calculator site's table, not a standard); the motor's nameplate or maker gives the true figure, so the lesson uses it only as a labelled practice value.

A breaker to BS EN 60898 has a conventional tripping current of 1.45 In within 1 hour (up to 63 A), so I2 = 1.45 In; a thermal overload relay is not one of those devices, so its own characteristic must be checked against Iz; the slides (p.30) say it takes 10,000 s, which is where Appendix 3's curves end rather than the conventional time. For breakers and gG fuses, Regulation 433.1.201 says that meeting Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz also meets I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz.

Lightly loaded cables leave the group: a cable expected to carry no more than 30 % of its grouped rating may be ignored when finding the group factor for the rest of the group (Table 4C1 note 9), the point of C&G practice paper 1 question 10b.

A hazard of overload is overheating of the circuit conductors, which over time damages insulation, joints and terminations and their surroundings and can lead to fire; BS 7671 also expects a circuit to be designed so that a small overload of long duration is unlikely.

His project guide points to "section 4.7 of The Electrical Installation Guide" for the motor question; which book that is could not be established, so the lesson cites the starter makers and Table 4C1 instead.

For i3 (review fixes): the maker's catalogue gives type B breakers to IEC/EN 60898-1 from 6 to 63 A operation within 1 hour at 1.45 In, while the slides (p.30) say a device at I2 can take 10,000 s: the sources differ on the time. Table 4E1A note 1 (his copy p.458) rates 90 °C cables at the lower temperature of the equipment they connect to; at 70 °C, Table 4D1A column 5 (his copy p.448) gives 1.5 mm² 15.5 A.
